_readme: Build eval/relevance_pool.json: for every golden fault, a wide candidate pool of KB chunks
labelled relevant / wrong_fault / irrelevant by an LLM judge.

faults.description: Lumbar flexion (butt wink): posterior pelvic tilt and rounding of the lower back at the bottom of the squat
queries: Lumbar flexion (butt wink): posterior pelvic tilt and rounding of the lower back at the bottom of the squat
butt wink during the squat
Why butt wink matters in the squat: which joint or muscle takes the extra load and what it risks
How to correct butt wink in the squat: cues, setup changes, drills and correct form

chunks.text: Ensure the spine and pelvis remain in a neutral, fully supported position during the hip quadrant test, allowing only the tested lower extremity to move.
chunks.source: data\squat\ANTHROPOMETRICAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR CUSTOMIZING THE SQUAT PATTERN.pdf [part 2/4]
chunks.label: irrelevant
chunks.reason: Describes protocol for the hip quadrant test, not the squat.

chunks.text: Test degrees of hip flexion, external rotation, and abduction synergistically to find the maximum pain-free hip flexion angle, which represents the anatomical limit for squat depth.
chunks.source: data\squat\ANTHROPOMETRICAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR CUSTOMIZING THE SQUAT PATTERN.pdf [part 2/4]
chunks.label: irrelevant
chunks.reason: Describes hip mobility testing protocol rather than the fault itself.

chunks.text: Allowing compensation patterns in the pelvis, spine, or opposite extremity during hip mobility testing.
chunks.source: data\squat\ANTHROPOMETRICAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR CUSTOMIZING THE SQUAT PATTERN.pdf [part 2/4]
chunks.label: irrelevant
chunks.reason: Addresses compensation during hip mobility testing, not during the squat.

chunks.text: Ignoring individual anatomical variations in femoral version and acetabular orientation when prescribing squat stance and depth.
chunks.source: data\squat\ANTHROPOMETRICAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR CUSTOMIZING THE SQUAT PATTERN.pdf [part 2/4]
chunks.label: irrelevant
chunks.reason: General statement about anatomy and squat prescription without mentioning the fault.

chunks.text: Exceeding the hip joint's anatomical limit (the theoretical glass ceiling on squat depth) forces compensation patterns, such as posterior pelvic tilt and spinal rounding.
chunks.source: data\squat\ANTHROPOMETRICAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR CUSTOMIZING THE SQUAT PATTERN.pdf [part 2/4]
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Explains how exceeding hip anatomical depth limits causes posterior pelvic tilt and spinal rounding.

chunks.text: Squat stance width and toe-out angle should be customized based on the individual's hip anatomy to maximize comfort, depth, and proper execution.
chunks.source: data\squat\ANTHROPOMETRICAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR CUSTOMIZING THE SQUAT PATTERN.pdf [part 3/4]
chunks.label: irrelevant
chunks.reason: General advice on customizing squat stance width and toe-out angle.

chunks.text: If maximal hip flexion is achieved with relatively more hip abduction during assessment, a wider squat stance may be more ideal for the athlete.
chunks.source: data\squat\ANTHROPOMETRICAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR CUSTOMIZING THE SQUAT PATTERN.pdf [part 3/4]
chunks.label: irrelevant
chunks.reason: General guidance on stance width based on hip assessment findings.

chunks.text: The degree of toe-out or external rotation at the hip joint should be adjusted to match the angle where maximal comfortable hip flexion is achieved.
chunks.source: data\squat\ANTHROPOMETRICAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR CUSTOMIZING THE SQUAT PATTERN.pdf [part 3/4]
chunks.label: irrelevant
chunks.reason: General advice on adjusting toe-out angle for hip comfort.

chunks.text: Squatting with a stance width or foot abduction angle that does not match the individual's anatomical capacity can lead to premature lumbar flexion.
chunks.source: data\squat\ANTHROPOMETRICAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR CUSTOMIZING THE SQUAT PATTERN.pdf [part 3/4]
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Explains how mismatched stance width or foot angle leads to lumbar flexion.

chunks.text: Forcing deep hip flexion without accommodating the necessary hip abduction and external rotation causes the pelvis to tilt posteriorly and the lumbar spine to flex.
chunks.source: data\squat\ANTHROPOMETRICAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR CUSTOMIZING THE SQUAT PATTERN.pdf [part 3/4]
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Identifies how restricted hip mechanics cause posterior pelvic tilt and lumbar flexion.

chunks.text: Athlete comfort should dictate the combination of stance width and toe-out, provided that biomechanical faults like knees collapsing in, lumbar flexion, or heels elevating are avoided.
chunks.source: data\squat\ANTHROPOMETRICAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR CUSTOMIZING THE SQUAT PATTERN.pdf [part 4/4]
chunks.label: irrelevant
chunks.reason: General stance guidance that only mentions lumbar flexion in a list of faults.

chunks.text: Allowing lumbar flexion during a squat is a biomechanical fault that must be avoided.
chunks.source: data\squat\ANTHROPOMETRICAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR CUSTOMIZING THE SQUAT PATTERN.pdf [part 4/4]
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Directly identifies lumbar flexion during a squat as a fault to avoid.

chunks.text: The lumbar vertebrae should be maintained in a neutral alignment throughout the entire squat movement, which entails keeping a slight lordotic curve in the lumbar region while holding the abdomen upward and rigid.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Specifies maintaining neutral lumbar lordosis to prevent lumbar flexion during squats.

chunks.text: The individual must maintain a stiffened torso with a neutral, lordotic lumbar position as a safe and optimal squat strategy.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Core form principle of maintaining a neutral, lordotic lumbar position to prevent flexion.

chunks.text: Failing to stiffen the lower back musculature and allowing the trunk to collapse downward into excessive flexion is a common deficit.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Describes excessive downward trunk flexion/collapse rather than butt wink.

chunks.text: Losing the neutral curvature of the lumbar spine during the squat is a common deficit.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Directly identifies losing neutral lumbar curvature (lumbar flexion) as a squat deficit.

chunks.text: Losing the neutral curve of the lumbar spine causes the spine to lose its ability to bear load, preventing safe progression of the squat with load.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Explains the consequence of lumbar flexion on spinal load-bearing capacity.

chunks.text: The squat requires sufficient spinal mobility to assume and maintain a slight lordotic posture.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Identifies the spinal mobility needed to maintain lumbar lordosis and avoid flexion.

chunks.text: The athlete must stiffen the back musculature to support the spine positioned in a neutral, slightly lordotic position.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Describes muscular stiffening to maintain a neutral, lordotic spine and prevent flexion.

chunks.text: The athlete should maintain a slight lordotic curve in the lumbar spine and keep the trunk angle parallel with the tibial angles.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Prescribes maintaining a slight lordotic curve in the lumbar spine during squats.

chunks.text: Executing a squat to at least parallel with only a dowel as external resistance allows a coach to gauge when and if the athlete presents excessive anterior or posterior pelvic tilt.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Describes using a dowel squat to identify excessive posterior pelvic tilt.

chunks.text: Excessive trunk flexion and/or rounding (kyphosis) of the spine can occur during the back squat due to relaxed back musculature and spinal flexion.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Refers to excessive trunk flexion and thoracic rounding (kyphosis), a different fault.

chunks.text: An athlete may flex at the spine before 120 degrees of hip flexion when squatting.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Describes spinal flexion occurring prematurely during hip flexion in the squat.

chunks.text: If the athlete flexes at the spine before 120 degrees of hip flexion when squatting, they may have restriction in the posterior fibers of the iliotibial band or lack of lumbar control.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Explains causes of spinal flexion during the squat.

chunks.text: Failing to stiffen the back musculature to support a neutral, slightly lordotic spine may result in increased and potentially harmful compressive and shear forces on the lumbar spine.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Explains the harmful compressive and shear forces resulting from losing lumbar lordosis.

chunks.text: Squatting with the spine in a flexed position increases the risk of disc herniation as a result of excessive stress placed on intervertebral discs.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Identifies disc herniation risk from squatting with a flexed spine.

chunks.text: Insufficient spinal or hip mobility may cause an individual to take a forward posture and place excessive pressure on the lower back.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Relates to excessive forward lean, a different fault in the squat.

chunks.text: Maintaining a neutral pelvic tilt during the squat increases activity of the erector spinae and oblique muscles, helping to ensure optimal muscular support for the spine.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Explains the muscular support benefits of maintaining a neutral pelvis in squats.

chunks.text: The athlete should maintain the pelvis in a normal or neutral tilt, particularly during the descent phase and in the final part of the descent.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Provides correct form instruction to maintain neutral pelvic tilt through squat descent.

chunks.text: Failing to maintain a neutral pelvic tilt reduces muscular support for the spine while handling loads, which increases the risk for low back injury.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Explains the injury risk of failing to maintain neutral pelvic tilt.

chunks.text: Use the pelvic rock test to identify the optimal width for the feet and knees to allow deep squatting without compromising back curvature.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Describes an assessment to find stance width that prevents back flexion in deep squats.

chunks.text: Allowing the neutral spine curvature to flex during a deep squat.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Directly describes the fault of spinal flexion during a deep squat.

chunks.text: The pelvic rock test starts with knees together, rocks the pelvis back toward the heels, and is repeated with knees spread apart a few inches to identify the point where neutral spine curvature begins to flex.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Describes how to identify the threshold where spine curvature flexes during deep squatting.

chunks.text: Allowing the spine to flex during a squat compromises back curvature and can lead to eventual pain and suboptimal performance.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Describes consequences of allowing the spine to flex during a squat.

chunks.text: The appropriate squat depth is the deepest position a client can achieve while maintaining a neutral spine, foot stability, proper joint alignment, and movement control.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Defines depth threshold based on maintaining a neutral spine to avoid flexion.

chunks.text: Posterior pelvic tilt ('butt wink') where the pelvis tucks under and the low back rounds at the bottom of a squat.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Direct definition and description of butt wink.

chunks.text: Forcing clients into an arbitrary squat depth standard rather than focusing on their individual anatomy, mobility, and ability to maintain a neutral spine.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Identifies forcing arbitrary depth beyond neutral spine capacity as a cause of the fault.

chunks.text: Proper cueing is the maintenance of a rigid spine that is either neutral or slightly flattened.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Provides cueing for spinal rigidity and neutrality to avoid spinal flexion.

chunks.text: Maintain a rigid spine by keeping constant contact with a dowel along the sacrum, thoracic spine, and back of the head throughout the movement.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Provides a dowel drill to maintain neutral spine and prevent rounding during squats.

chunks.text: Maintain a neutral low back position with a slight lordosis throughout the squat movement.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Specifies maintaining neutral low back lordosis throughout the squat to prevent butt wink.

chunks.text: Losing lumbar lordosis during the squat movement.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Directly describes the fault of losing lumbar lordosis (butt wink) during squats.

chunks.text: Intravertebral disc pressure increases as lumbar lordosis is lost, putting the lifter at risk for injury.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Explains the injury risk and spinal disc pressure caused by losing lumbar lordosis.

chunks.text: Use a hip hinge drill holding a dowel along the length of the spine to cue and maintain a neutral spine position while descending.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Describes a drill to cue neutral spine and prevent lumbar flexion during descent.

chunks.text: Failing to properly descend while pivoting at the hips and maintaining a correct lumbar position.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Describes failing to maintain lumbar alignment during the descent of the squat.

chunks.text: Bending the spine and not keeping it straight and aligned with your pelvis.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Describes spinal bending and failure to keep the spine aligned with the pelvis.

chunks.text: Maintain an upright chest and thoracic position with the scapula retracted to attain a correct lumbo-pelvic position.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Focuses on thoracic and scapular positioning, addressing upper-body posture rather than butt wink.

chunks.text: Perform a static chest stretch on a foam roll to lengthen tight anterior chest muscles, which allows for proper scapular strengthening.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Provides a corrective stretch for anterior chest tightness and scapular issues, not butt wink.

chunks.text: Failing to maintain an upright chest and thoracic position due to tight anterior chest muscles.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Addresses thoracic collapse and chest posture rather than lumbar flexion or posterior pelvic tilt.

chunks.text: Tight anterior chest muscles prevent proper scapular retraction, making it difficult to maintain an upright chest and correct lumbo-pelvic position.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Explains mechanisms of upper-body/thoracic posture breakdown rather than lumbar butt wink.

chunks.text: Your trunk and pelvis should stay neutral and aligned as you bend at your hips, with your pelvis remaining in a neutral position without tucking under or tilting backward.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Directly describes maintaining a neutral pelvis without tucking under or tilting backward.

chunks.text: Limited range of motion in the hips, knees, ankles, or lumbar spine can cause your tailbone to tuck under at the bottom of the movement, a compensation commonly known as butt wink.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Directly explains mobility causes of tailbone tucking at the bottom (butt wink).

chunks.text: Compensations such as tailbone tucking (butt wink), heels lifting, or incorrect knee tracking due to limited mobility can increase the risk of injury.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Explicitly identifies tailbone tucking (butt wink) and states its injury risk.

chunks.text: Keep your spine straight and aligned with your pelvis, remaining relatively straight and parallel to your shins.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Cues proper spinal and pelvic alignment throughout the squat movement.

chunks.text: If you lack the appropriate mobility at your hips, knees, or ankles to maintain proper alignment during a deep squat, perform a squat in which your hips do not go below your knees.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Recommends limiting squat depth to prevent alignment breakdown and butt wink.

chunks.text: Not keeping your spine straight and aligned with your pelvis increases the risk of strain and shear force in the spine.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: Explains the injury consequences of failing to keep the spine aligned with the pelvis.

chunks.text: Failing to keep the spine straight and extended increases the risk of injury to the spine or intervertebral discs.
chunks.label: relevant
chunks.reason: States the spinal and disc injury risks of failing to maintain spinal extension.

chunks.text: Demonstrating decreased hip flexion during the squat cycle.
chunks.source: data\squat\Muscle Activation Patterns During Different Squat Techniques.pdf [part 5/12]
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Describes a different fault regarding insufficient hip flexion and squat depth.

chunks.text: Excessive anterior translation of the knees over the toes during the squat.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Describes a different fault involving excessive forward knee translation over the toes.

chunks.text: Squatting with limited weight-bearing ankle dorsiflexion range of motion, which restricts sagittal-plane motion at the knee and ankle.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Describes limited ankle dorsiflexion and restricted knee/ankle sagittal motion, a different fault.

chunks.text: Squatting with limited ankle dorsiflexion range of motion, which restricts forward rotation of the shank.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Describes limited ankle dorsiflexion restricting shank rotation, a different fault.

chunks.text: Excessive thoracic forward lean during the descent.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: About excessive thoracic forward lean, not lumbar flexion or butt wink.

chunks.text: Heels rising or feet turning out during the squat, which frequently indicates limited ankle dorsiflexion.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: About heels rising or feet turning out, not butt wink.

chunks.text: Internal rotation of the femurs during descent, which may be caused by tight hip adductors.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: About internal rotation of the femurs, not lumbar flexion.

chunks.text: Overly restricted tibial translation during the squat.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: About restricted tibial translation, a different squat fault.

chunks.text: Adopting a head-up position during the upward phase of the squat, which can exacerbate spinal extension.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: About head position and spinal extension, not posterior pelvic tilt.

chunks.text: Allowing the knees to displace medially and anteriorly, resulting in a medio-lateral malaligned squat.
chunks.source: data\squat\Muscle Activation Patterns During Different Squat Techniques.pdf [part 4/12]
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: About medial and anterior knee displacement, not butt wink.

chunks.text: Squatting with limited ankle dorsiflexion range of motion, which restricts knee and ankle sagittal-plane displacement and results in smaller peak knee-flexion angles.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: About limited ankle dorsiflexion restricting knee flexion, not butt wink.

chunks.text: Performing squats with limited ankle dorsiflexion range of motion, which is associated with medial knee displacement.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: About medial knee displacement related to ankle dorsiflexion.

chunks.text: Allowing the knees to cave inward (medial knee displacement) during the squat.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: About knee valgus (medial knee displacement), not butt wink.

chunks.text: Attempting to squat with limited weight-bearing ankle dorsiflexion range of motion, which restricts the depth of the squat.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: About restricted squat depth from limited ankle dorsiflexion.

chunks.text: Allowing mediolateral malalignment of the knees during the squat descent and ascent.
chunks.source: data\squat\Muscle Activation Patterns During Different Squat Techniques.pdf [part 6/12]
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: About mediolateral knee malalignment, not lumbar flexion.

chunks.text: Performing deep squats beyond 50 degrees of knee flexion when suffering from patellofemoral pain, which can provoke pain due to high compressive loads.
chunks.source: data\squat\Physiotherapy Res Intl - 2015 - Jaberzadeh - The Effect of Altering Knee Position and Squat Depth on VMO   VL EMG Ratio.pdf [part 8/10]
chunks.label: irrelevant
chunks.reason: General clinical guidance for patellofemoral pain, not about butt wink.

chunks.text: Displacing the knee excessively in the anterior-posterior or medio-lateral directions during the squat.
chunks.source: data\squat\Muscle Activation Patterns During Different Squat Techniques.pdf [part 1/12]
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: About excessive knee displacement in AP or ML directions.

chunks.text: Restricted translation of the knees during the squat may increase anterior forward lean of the trunk.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: About restricted knee translation causing trunk forward lean, not butt wink.

chunks.text: Allowing too much anterior knee displacement during the squat.
chunks.source: data\squat\Muscle Activation Patterns During Different Squat Techniques.pdf [part 8/12]
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: About excessive anterior knee displacement, a different squat fault.

chunks.text: Restricting anterior knee displacement excessively during the squat.
chunks.source: data\squat\Muscle Activation Patterns During Different Squat Techniques.pdf [part 8/12]
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: About excessively restricting anterior knee displacement.

chunks.text: Performing an anteroposterior (AP) malaligned squat.
chunks.source: data\squat\Muscle Activation Patterns During Different Squat Techniques.pdf [part 8/12]
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: About anteroposterior malalignment, not butt wink.

chunks.text: Demonstrating a compensatory movement pattern of increased trunk flexion due to a lack of hip mobility.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: About excessive trunk flexion rather than lumbar flexion or posterior pelvic tilt.

chunks.text: Allowing the knees to cave inward medially during the squat.
chunks.source: data\squat\Muscle Activation Patterns During Different Squat Techniques.pdf [part 1/12]
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: About knee caving inward (valgus), not butt wink.

chunks.text: Squatting to a depth of 75 to 90 degrees of knee flexion when suffering from patellofemoral pain.
chunks.label: irrelevant
chunks.reason: Specific depth guideline for patellofemoral pain, not about butt wink.

chunks.text: Adopting an excessive head-up position to compensate for inadequate hip flexor or ankle mobility.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Addresses excessive head-up position and cervical hyperextension, not butt wink.

chunks.text: Performing squats with the knees collapsing inward, representing mediolateral malalignment.
chunks.source: data\squat\Muscle Activation Patterns During Different Squat Techniques.pdf [part 3/12]
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Describes knee valgus (inward knee collapse), which is a different squat fault.

chunks.text: Consciously restricting forward translation of the knees past the toes, which alters squat mechanics.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Describes restricting forward knee travel, a different movement fault.

chunks.text: Excessive forward lean during the squat, which is commonly associated with limited ankle mobility, limited hip mobility, and underactive anterior core musculature.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Describes excessive forward trunk lean, which is a different squat fault.

chunks.text: Knees caving in (knee valgus) during the squat, which is commonly associated with overactive adductors, overactive tensor fasciae latae (TFL), and underactive gluteus medius and gluteus maximus.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Describes knee valgus (inward knee collapse), a different squat fault.

chunks.text: Allowing the knees to collapse inward, also known as medial knee displacement, during the squat.
chunks.source: data\squat\Muscle Activation Patterns During Different Squat Techniques.pdf [part 2/12]
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Describes medial knee displacement (knee valgus), a different squat fault.

chunks.text: Having limited ankle dorsiflexion range of motion, which restricts the displacement of both the ankle and knee joints during the squat.
chunks.label: irrelevant
chunks.reason: General biomechanical observation about ankle mobility and joint displacement.

chunks.text: Losing descent control toward the later phases of the movement, which is common in athletes with insufficient posterior chain strength.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Describes uncontrolled descent (dive-bombing), a different squat fault.

chunks.text: Using a knee-loading strategy instead of a hip-hinge strategy during descent, which is seen with excessive trunk flexion, excessive tibial progression angle, and/or heels coming off of the ground.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Describes knee-dominant descent strategy and heels lifting, different faults.

chunks.text: Knee valgus is identified when the medial aspect of either knee passes the medial malleolus from the anterior perspective during any phase of the squat.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Defines criteria for identifying knee valgus, a different squat fault.

chunks.text: Allowing the hips to rise faster than the shoulders during the early ascent phase, which increases trunk flexion and decreases the vertical distance between the hips and shoulders.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Describes hips rising faster than shoulders (good-morning squat), a different fault.

chunks.text: Failing to reach parallel squat depth.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Describes failing to reach parallel depth (shallow squatting), a different fault.

chunks.text: The hips rise too quickly in relation to the shoulders during the ascent of the squat.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Describes hips rising too quickly on ascent, a different squat fault.

chunks.text: Lacking hip mobility causes a compensatory movement pattern of increased trunk flexion during the squat.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Describes excessive trunk flexion (forward lean), a different squat fault.

chunks.text: Maintaining a slight upward gaze throughout the squat may help prevent excessive forward trunk flexion.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Cues gaze to prevent excessive forward trunk lean, a different fault.

chunks.text: Squatting with limited ankle dorsiflexion restricts knee forward travel and knee flexion, leading to a shallower squat.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Describes limited depth (shallow squat), which is a different fault.

chunks.text: Hips rising too quickly during the ascent indicates weakness in the posterior chain and hip extension concentric muscle action.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Describes hips rising too quickly (good-morning squat), a different fault.

chunks.text: Allowing the chest to drop or failing to retract the scapulae during the squat is a common deficit.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Describes chest drop and scapular retraction failure, a different fault.

chunks.text: Squat depth should be determined based on the position of the hips.
chunks.label: irrelevant
chunks.reason: General guideline on squat depth; too vague to relate to butt wink.

chunks.text: Allowing the knees to cave inward into a valgus position during the squat.
chunks.source: data\squat\Physiotherapy Res Intl - 2015 - Jaberzadeh - The Effect of Altering Knee Position and Squat Depth on VMO   VL EMG Ratio.pdf [part 1/10]
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Describes knee valgus (inward knee cave), a different squat fault.

chunks.text: Breaking the hips at the initiation of the squat movement migrates the load to the posterior chain, which is a more safe strategy for the knees and lumbar vertebrae.
chunks.label: irrelevant
chunks.reason: General cue about squat initiation and load distribution, not butt wink.

chunks.text: Allowing the eye gaze to move upward with a head tilt during the squat.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Refers to head and gaze alignment faults, not lumbar flexion.

chunks.text: Overly restricted tibial translation during the squat increases anterior lean of the torso, which increases hip torque and lumbar shear forces.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Discusses restricted tibial translation causing excessive trunk lean, a different fault.

chunks.text: Limiting tibial translation during a squat can cause an increase in trunk anterior lean to compensate.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Addresses excessive anterior trunk lean caused by limited knee travel.

chunks.text: Restricting anterior knee displacement can result in increased thoracic motion and forces at the hip and back during squats.
chunks.source: data\squat\Muscle Activation Patterns During Different Squat Techniques.pdf [part 7/12]
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Discusses restricted knee displacement and thoracic movement, not butt wink.

chunks.text: Maintaining adequate weight-bearing ankle dorsiflexion range of motion is essential for achieving proper knee-flexion displacement and sagittal-plane depth during squatting tasks.
chunks.label: irrelevant
chunks.reason: General statement about ankle dorsiflexion requirements for squat depth.

chunks.text: Avoid excessive anterior knee displacement during squats to manage patellofemoral contact forces.
chunks.source: data\squat\Muscle Activation Patterns During Different Squat Techniques.pdf [part 8/12]
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Addresses excessive anterior knee displacement, a different fault.

chunks.text: Limited ankle dorsiflexion restricts knee flexion displacement, which directly prevents the lifter from reaching full squat depth.
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Discusses failure to achieve full squat depth, a different fault.

chunks.text: Using compensatory movement strategies during the squat due to improper mechanics.
chunks.label: irrelevant
chunks.reason: Too vague; does not name or describe butt wink or its mechanics.

chunks.text: Avoid excessively restricting anterior knee displacement during squats to prevent excessive forces at the hip and back.
chunks.source: data\squat\Muscle Activation Patterns During Different Squat Techniques.pdf [part 8/12]
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Addresses restricted anterior knee travel, not lumbar flexion at the bottom.

chunks.text: A poorly performed squat with increased knee valgus may expose the lower extremity joints to excessive torques.
chunks.source: data\squat\Muscle Activation Patterns During Different Squat Techniques.pdf [part 1/12]
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: About knee valgus, a completely different fault.

chunks.text: Allowing medio-lateral malalignment during the squat, which alters the activation of the quadriceps, hamstrings, and gastrocnemius muscles.
chunks.source: data\squat\Muscle Activation Patterns During Different Squat Techniques.pdf [part 5/12]
chunks.label: wrong_fault
chunks.reason: Addresses medio-lateral knee malalignment (valgus/varus), not butt wink.

chunks.text: The 80° knee flexed angle condition resulted in greater peak joint reaction force and extensor moment compared with both 90° and 100° conditions between the upward and downward phases of the forward lunge.

chunks.text: A shallower front knee flexion angle of 80° increases the peak joint reaction forces and extensor moments on the knee joint compared to deeper angles of 90° and 100°.

chunks.text: Achieving a knee flexion angle of 90 degrees or greater (such as 100 degrees) on the front leg during a forward lunge reduces the knee extensor moment compared to a shallower 80-degree angle.

chunks.text: A deeper knee flexion angle of 100 degrees reduces lateral and vertical joint reaction forces compared to shallower angles of 80 and 90 degrees.
chunks.source: data\lunge\Effects of Targeted Knee Flexion Angle on the Biomechanical Factors of Upward and Downward Phases during Forward Lunge.pdf [part 5/11]
